notes: \cpara{Opens with a childhood memory: the author was told that a Hebrew prayer works whether or not you know what the words mean.}
\cpara{Dates the author's break with Judaism to that moment.}
\cpara{A typical case, told as a joke: a student studies ``12th-century knitting patterns'' only because the degree, and the job, require it.}
\cpara{Tells the reader they probably did the same.}

\cpara{The first case, schools. The figures match the \textsc{San Francisco Chronicle}'s report of a survey of 923 Bay Area teachers by the Lawrence Hall of Science and WestEd: ``About 80 percent'' spent less than an hour a week on science, and ``About 16 percent'' none. The report supports the hedged link to No Child Left Behind: most of the 16 percent taught at schools that ``had missed the reading and math benchmarks.''}

\cfact{Stated without a hedge or a source, and overstated. A national survey of school districts from the same year (Center on Education Policy, 2007) found that elementary schools still spent on average 178 minutes a week on science and 178 on social studies. It also found the trend the post describes: 44\% of districts had cut time from other subjects to add time for reading and mathematics, the subjects the Act tests.}

\cpara{The second case, Soviet factories that met quotas in appearance only: tiny shoes, and cut leather counted as shoes. The first story has no source. The link for the second goes to a page of Meyer Kron's memoir on a Concordia University site that I could not reach, so I could not check it.}

\cpara{The third case, medical research, stated with ``It is now being suggested.'' The hedge fits the source. The linked paper, Ioannidis's ``Why Most Published Research Findings Are False'' (2005), reports that ``Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true''; it is a model, not a count of false findings. It names small studies among the causes, as the post's point about ``larger experimental groups'' implies.}
\cpara{A joke that physics has another purpose than publishing papers.}

\cfact{The fact behind it is loosely stated. I found no journal threshold of p<0.0001. The known convention is in particle physics, and is stricter: to claim a ``discovery,'' the p-value must be ``no larger than $3 \times 10^{-7}$,'' and ``journals are very reluctant'' to print the word otherwise (Louis Lyons, ``Discovering the Significance of 5$\sigma$,'' 2013). It governs claims of discovery, not publication.}
\cpara{The individual case: a person who finds no chocolate at the supermarket does not keep opening the car door. The author ``rarely'' sees people lose track of plans they made themselves.}
\cpara{Contrasts organizations, where someone may be paid for each opening of the car door, because that is what can be measured.}
\cpara{Restates the point of ``Terminal Values and Instrumental Values'' (15 November 2007): a subgoal's value comes only from what it leads to.}
\cpara{Traces the Act's chain of incentives: politicians and bureaucrats reward what shows progress this year, and none of them sits in the classroom.}

\cpara{Continues down the chain to parents, textbook publishers, purchasing committees and teachers. Each link is described as fact and without a source. The most specific claims, that committees for different grades are not coordinated and that teachers ``won't get through a fourth of the textbook,'' come with no evidence.}
\cpara{Marvels that any learning survives.}

\clogic{``Collapsing into a state not much better than nothing'' is offered with ``seem'' and no evidence. For the United States, the case the post discusses, the national assessment reported in 2007 that fourth-graders scored higher than in any earlier year: in mathematics ``27 points higher than in 1990,'' in reading ``higher than in any of the previous assessment years'' (NAEP 2007). Test scores are the kind of measure the post distrusts, but these figures sit uneasily with a collapse.}
\cpara{A joke: make the politicians go to school.}

\cpara{States the general thesis: one mind can follow expected value through many steps, but organizations can reward only what is measurable today, and their measures are leaky. Links it to ``The Hidden Complexity of Wishes'': bureaucrats are genies that do not share the wisher's values.}

\clogic{The organizational half of this is an old point in social science, and the post does not mention it. Donald Campbell wrote in 1976 that when test scores ``become the goal of the teaching process, they both lose their value as indicators of educational status and distort the educational process in undesirable ways'' (as quoted in Wikipedia, ``Campbell's law''). What the post adds is the contrast with a single mind.}
\cpara{Introduces a quotation from Musashi.}

\cpara{Quotes \textsc{The Book of Five Rings}, in Victor Harris's translation; the wording matches. Every movement of the sword must be carried through to cutting the enemy. ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality'' quotes the same passage.}
\cpara{An aside on Musashi's instruction to research this thoroughly.}
\cpara{Explains how an individual can lose purpose: by learning an art from others without knowing why each rule holds.}
\cpara{Applies Musashi to reasoning and decision: see how every rule cuts through to truth, and every expected utility to utility.}
\cpara{Introduces a second quotation, from the novelist C. J. Cherryh. The post does not name the book, and I could not check the wording.}
\cpara{Applies the idea to people who draft wishes for an imagined AI: unlike the author, who asks ``reflexively,'' they do not ask why they think a wish is good.}
\cpara{Adds a second failure to notice: selfish people giving altruistic arguments, and the reverse.}
\cpara{Says that between a child in class and a graduate at work lie dozens of organizations and years, and each link loses information and incentive.}

\clogic{The evidence that this ``bothers most people a lot less'' is the author's classmates in kindergarten or first grade, who said prayers without knowing their meaning. That is thin evidence about adults.}
\cpara{Asks whether people, corporations or a civilization can learn to keep track of purposes, and says this is what the recent series of posts has been about.}
\cpara{Calls complexity ``the worst metathreat to complex civilization.'' The ranking is asserted; no other threat is compared.}
\cpara{Ends with the author's own trait, ``an exceptionally strong abhorrence to lost purposes,'' and the hope that it can be taught. The evidence for the trait is the author's own report.}
